text: Stereochemistry-directed solvent molecular design for advanced Lithium-Sulfur batteries Dexiang Xu a,b, Zifeng Liu b, Fuyong Liu b, Miao Chen b, Dan Zhou b, Zhubing Xiao a,b,* a Key Laboratory of Green and Precise Synthetic Chemistry and Applications, Ministry of Education, Anhui Key Laboratory of Synthetic Chemistry and Applications, School of Chemistry and Materials Science, Huaibei Normal University, Huaibei, Anhui 235000, PR China b Henan Key Laboratory of Quantum Materials and Quantum Energy, School of Future Technology, Henan University, Henan, Zhengzhou 450046, PR China A R T I C L E I N F O Keywords: Li-S batteries Electrolyte engineering Solvation structure Polysulfides Li compatibility A B S T R A C T Li-S batteries are attractive due to its high energy density, while its application is severely hindered by the sluggish kinetics and notorious side reactions between the soluble polysulfides and lithium metal anode.

Herein, the concept of steric tuning electrolyte is proposed to facilitate the sulfur redox reaction and maintain a superb metallic Li compatibility via utilizing suitable methyl propyl ether as co-solvent for electrolyte-starved energydense Li-S batteries.

By combining ab-initio molecular dynamics simulations, spectral characterization, and insitu measurements of the electrochemical cell, it is confirmed that the stereochemistry manipulation endows the electrolyte with a weakened solvation ability to enhance the reaction kinetics and forms an encapsulated polysulfide solvation structure to prohibit the anode parasitic reactions from polysulfides.
In virtue of the optimized local environment of STE, the Li-S cells deliver significantly improved electrochemical performance under lean electrolyte conditions.
Moreover, the Li-S cells could stably operates under −30 ◦C for 100 cycles at 0.5C, which may promote the practical application in cold environment. 1.
Introduction Lithium-sulfur (Li-S) batteries have emerged as a promising energy storage system, capturing significant attention in recent years.
Their immense appeal stems from the impressive theoretical capacity and the use of sulfur–a low-cost, abundant, and environmentally benign mate­ rial [1–4].
Nevertheless, the pathway to their commercialization is fraught with challenges.

Among these, the infamous “shuttle effect” stands out, where soluble lithium polysulfides (LiPS) migrate between the electrodes, leading to rapid capacity decay and self-discharge, especially for the cell operation under lean electrolyte condition [5–8].
Moreover, the inherent sluggish kinetics associated with the multi-step conversion of sulfur redox reaction (SRR) poses a significant hurdle to achieving high rate performance [9–12].
Additionally, in­ compatibility between the electrode materials and electrolyte compro­ mises both the cell’s overall efficiency and its lifespan [13].
These issues, while being actively researched, remain critical barriers that need to be conquered to boost the implementation of Li-S batteries [14–16].

Traditional strategies of physical confinement or chemical adsorp­ tion focus too much on the sulfur cathode [17–21], failing to solve the intertwined issues of Li metal anode, especially for the Li/electrolyte compatibility and the parasitical side reactions between the polysulfides (PS) and Li metal, both of which incur the loss of active materials, rapid capacity decay, and even safety concerns [22–24].

Electrolyte engi­ neering including solvent recipe modification and salt additive optimi­ zation provides a new platform to manipulate both the Li-S chemistry and solid-electrolyte interphase (SEI) structure, which generally fall within the categories of sparingly solvating electrolytes (SSE) and highly solvating electrolytes (HSE).
In the SSE class, the solvation of LiPS is largely ameliorated in the limited solvent and/or selective solvent, which requires the supporting salt to solvate more readily over the LiPS.
However, it also faces daunting challenges such as high viscosity, low ionic conductivity, high cell polarization, and sluggish redox reaction kinetics.
Adopting the opposite strategy, the HSE system provides a higher LiPS solubility at less electrolyte to achieve faster reaction ki­ netics.
But the high reactivity of PS with Li metal anode requires special protection for the anode side and robust construction of SEI to avoid the cell dry-out and failure [16,25–27].
It can be found that the adaptations in the two motifs often fall short of meeting rigorous standards for lean electrolyte usage in high-energy–density Li-S batteries.
Under this backdrop, focusing on regulating the LiPS solvation structure, the concept of encapsulated polysulfide electrolytes (EPSE) was proposed * Corresponding author.

recently to restrain the parasitic reactions of PS on Li metal anode, meanwhile maintaining decent kinetics of SRR as well as durability in energy-dense Li-S cells, which to some extent solves the dilemma in SSE and HSE strategies.

However, owing to the heterogeneous double-shell solvation structure constructed by the two concentric solvents, the EPSE-based Li-S batteries usually suffer from large cell polarization, poor rate performance, unsatisfactory utilization of active materials, and finally inferior energy density at the pouch cell level, failing to meet the ever-increasing energy demand [28–31].

Therefore, more exquisite solvation structure engineering and mechanistic understanding of the relationship between the solvation structure of LiPS and the reaction kinetics are urgently needed for synchronously addressing the cathode and anode issues towards practically available Li-S batteries.

As a proof-of-concept study to address the above-mentioned chal­ lenges in electrolyte engineering of Li-S batteries, herein, we propose the concept of steric tuning electrolyte (STE) to substantially accelerate the cathode sulfur reaction kinetics and maintain a superb metallic Li compatibility as well as mechanically robust SEI layer under lean elec­ trolyte condition via incorporating suitable methyl propyl ether (MPE).

With the manipulation of stereochemistry, the steric hindrance effect of ether solvent molecules and the LiPS solvation structure are dramati­ cally optimized, which results in a stronger protection of the Li metal anode and promoted kinetics of SRR.

Benefiting from the ameliorated local environment of STE, the electrolyte-starved Li-S cells deliver decent electrochemical performance at high sulfur loading, which is expected to promote the practical application of energy-dense Li-S batteries.
Moreover, the Li-S cells could still operate well under the gelid condition, which may promote the practical application in cold environment. 2.
Materials and electrode preparations The high conductive graphene (HCG) was purchased from Suzhou Tanfeng Graphene Technology Co.
For the HCG/S preparation, the S was infiltrated into HCG using a melt-diffusion strategy at 160 ◦C for 24 h, forming well-contacted and homogeneous HCG/S composites.
The cathode materials were prepared by mixing HCG/S, acetylene black, and polyvinylende fluoride (PVDF) binder in a weight ratio of 8: 1: 1 in Nmethyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP).
The slurry was then coated onto the aluminum foil and dried at 50 ◦C for 12 h.
Afterwards, the dried coated aluminum foil was punched into disks with a diameter of 14 mm for Li-S coin cell use, and the loading of the active-material was ~ 1.1 mg cm−2. 2.2.

Preparation of electrolyte Conventional electrolyte (CE), i.e., 1.0 M LiTFSI in 1,3-dioxolane (DOL)/ dimethoxyethane (DME) (1: 1, by vol.), and STE, i.e., 1.0 M LiTFSI in MPE/DOL/DME (4: 3: 3, by vol.), and 2 wt% LiNO3 was employed.
The electrolyte was prepared in an Ar-filled glove box. 3.

Results and discussion With an aim to screen a target solvent with relatively low solvation ability and relatively higher reduction stability, one of the O atoms in the dimethoxyethane (DME) solvent was tentatively substituted with a C atom to eliminate the chelation effect and provide the electron feedback to the H atoms, which results in the conceptual molecule of methyl butyl ether (MBE) (Fig. 1a) [32,33].
However, the high flexibility of longchain C enables MBE solvent with higher steric hindrance effect that should otherwise be avoided for achieving better reaction dynamics.
To this end, one C atom is further eliminated from the MBE molecular, which readily reaps the target of MPE.

Comparing with the traditional solvent of DME and 1,3-dioxolane (DOL), the MPE solvent carries a shorter chain and the decrease in O atom endows the H atom with a better ability to avoid the nucleophilic attack of PS with high reduction reactivity (Fig. 1a), which are highly favorable for propelling the reac­ tion kinetics of Li-S chemistry (vide infra).

Meanwhile, the shrinkage in molecular volume would endow MPE with less steric effect to accelerate Li+ de-solvation process and block the Li+-ether complex, thus increasing the reaction kinetics [32].

The MPE solvents, characterized by their smaller molecular size and reduced molecular polarity, stand out due to the uniquely tailored steric effects they present.
These inherent molecular attributes translate into a significant reduction in viscosity when compared to traditional DOL/DME electrolyte.
To qualitatively assess these viscosity properties, we employed the GROMACS simulation package to perform the viscosity simulations [36,37].
And its real value was tested by rheometer.
The incorporation amount of MPE (40 vol%) was first investigated to realize the best kinetic performance (Fig.
The viscosity simulation results and experimental test results jointly validate that the MPE-incorporated electrolyte exhibits ultra-low viscosity (Fig.
S2), which facilitates the ionic mass transfer within electrolyte, thus enhancing the overall effi­ ciency of the electrochemical processes involved in Li-S cells.

Addi­ tionally, this ultra-low viscosity would benefit the penetration of electrolyte into electrode, as evidenced by the diminutive contact angle between the electrode and MPE-incorporated electrolyte (Fig.

Theoretically, better wettability of the electrolyte on the material’s surface leads to improved interfacial kinetics and less electrolyte required to maintain the same reaction kinetics, which is advantageous for achieving better electrochemical performance under lean electrolyte condition, thus increasing the energy density of cell [38].
The inherent molecular properties of MPE were systematically investigated for an understanding of the function of target solvent.

By calculating the electrostatic potential (ESP), it is found that the electron density isosurface of MPE is more neutralized (Fig. 1b), indicating that the H atoms of MPE possess enhanced electronegativity while the O atom possess weakened electropositivity.
The ameliorated molecular polarization should benefit from the reduced O atom number.

Since the long-range secondary electrostatic interactions can be negligible in MPE molecule [39], the ESP behavior of MPE predicts that it not only helps reduce the side reactions brought by the disastrous nucleophilic attack by the PS species with high reduction reactivity but also contributes to a better compatibility between the electrolyte and Li anode.
We further utilized the Multiwfn software package to get a quantification analysis of the electrostatic reactions of the given solvent [28,40].
As can be seen in Fig. 1c, the areas of MPE solvent whose ESP energy is closer to zero account for a larger contribution percentage, consistent with the above direct visual results (Fig. 1b).
More interestingly, we found the lowest unoccupied molecular orbit (LUMO) energy level of MPE is elevated distinctly (Fig.
S4), which insinuates the improved reduction stability and better compatibility with both the PS species and Li anode [41,42], according to the frontier orbital theory.

This is also substantially vali­ dated by the reduction stability tests, where the MPE-incorporated saltfree electrolyte shows an ameliorated side reaction currents comparing with its counterpart (Fig. 1d).

After a systematic analysis of the stability and compatibility of MPE at a molecular scale, the solvation structures of electrolyte were further probed with quantum chemistry and molecular dynamics (MD) utilizing ORCA and GROMACS software, respectively.
Naturally, the elimination of chelation effect in MPE weakens the Li+ cation binding capability as can be vividly demonstrated by the binding energy calculation (Fig. 2a).

Though MPE solvent has a stronger binding energy relative to DOL, the MPE would still have weakened solvation capability because the two adjacent O atoms in DOL endows MPE with elevated possibilities to bind with Li+ [43].
As confirmed by the MD simulations (Fig. 2b), the collected radial distribution function (rdf) signifies that MPE solvent has a much smaller g(r) peak value comparing to DME and DOL solvents (Fig.
S6), which means that the solvation ability of Li+ follows the trend: DME > DOL > MPE.
The rdf results verify our hypothesis that the sol­ vation ability is related to both the binding energy and the numbers of atoms that coordinates to the Li+ [44].

The increased g(r) peak value of Li+-TFSI−after adding the MPE solvent further proves our hypothesis as an increased g(r) of the cation–anion can be traced to the weakened solvation ability of the electrolyte (Fig. 2c).
Given that the MPE solvent in electrolyte participates in the dissociation of lithium salts (Fig. 2c), there is a reasonable prospect that the MPE competitively participate in Fig. 2.

As witnessed in Fig. 2d, the MPE mainly exists in the second shell of the solvation structure, reaffirming the weak solvation ability of MPE [28,30].
As depicted in Fig.

S5, the peak intensities of both Li2S8 and Li2S4 in the UV–vis spectra are significantly reduced after addition of MPE, indicating the positive effect of suppressing polysulfide solubility owing to the weakly-solvating MPE.
Raman spectroscopy was employed to investigate the solvation structure of STE (Fig. 2e).
Peaks observed at approximately 820 and 850 cm−1 are attributed to the unbonded oxide bonds of isolated DME.

Remarkably, the intensity of these peaks associated with free DME di­ minishes upon the addition of the weakly coordinating MPE, suggesting that Li+ has a stronger affinity for DME in comparison with that in the DME/MPE mixed solvents [34,35].

Additionally, the Raman peak centered at 740 cm−1 arising from the S-N-S stretches of TFSI− [46] shows a clear blue-shift with the presence of MPE, upon which the interaction of Li+ of TFSI−is less impaired (Fig.

These Raman results confirm the fact that the solvent activity of DME solvent is substantially decreased by the addition of the weakly solvating MPE, meanwhile LiNO3 and LiTFSI would be preferentially reduced on the lithium sur­ face, which is underpinned by the 7Li nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) measurements.
When the Li2S8 was added into pure solvent mixtures of MPE/DME, the 7Li peak exhibits an appreciable down-shifts from −0.060 to −0.035 ppm (Fig.
S8), contributed by reduction of the overall binding energy of Li+ ions with solvent molecule [29].

This sparingly solvating power to a Li+ ions dictates the recruitment of MPE into the secondary sheath of a Li+ ions, which decreases the amounts of DME and DOL that are supposed to preferentially interact with Li+ ions, thus inducing the deshielding of Li+ ions.

Hence, the MPE molecules tend to distribute in the outer solvent shell around PS and the inner shell is mainly composed of DOL and DME [28], by which PS are encapsulated in anti-reductive solvent shells to decrease its reactivity towards Li anode, as schematically illustrated in Fig. 2f.

For a more intuitive comparison of the anti-reductive solvent struc­ ture and the Li de-solvation dynamics in STE, the numbers of Li+ ions with different solvation structure configurations were counted using MD simulations [47].
The snapshots obtained from MD simulations for conventional electrolyte (CE) and STE are displayed in Fig. 3a and 3b.

Given that the solvent-shell structure around Li+ is dynamic and diverse in electrolyte, we first examined each Li+ in the simulation systems and determined their O-donated solvated structure within a radius of 0.35 nm (the solvation shell boundary) by analyzing the MD trajectories in Fig. 3a and 3b.
To simulate the actual state of electrolyte working in Li-S batteries, we introduced a certain amount of LiPS into the simulation box.

It should be noted that the Li+-anion binding has generally been neglected in the de-solvation energy calculations in previous studies due to the repulsion from the significant negative polarization of the elec­ trode, as demonstrated by Fig. 3c.
For simplicity, we denoted three values after Li+ binding to represent the coordination numbers of DME, DOL, and MPE, respectively, for the collected solvation structures from the simulations.
For example, the abbreviation of Li300 stands for the Li+ coordination of three DME, zero DOL, and zero MPE molecule in the solvation structure.

As depic­ ted in Fig. 3f, the de-solvation free energy is markedly decreased with the presence of MPE, which is consolidated by our experimental mea­ surements according to fitting the temperature-dependent electro­ chemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) shown in Fig.

The above results indicate that the incorporation of MPE could optimize the electrolyte structure, in which the MPE molecules serve as the building blocks of the outer solvent shell where the parasitic reactions between the PS and Li metal are kinetically obstructed by the anti-reductive shell, thus promoting the kinetics of electrode reaction and mitigating its exposure to fresh Li.
The Li compatibility performances were further investigated by the Li||Cu and Li||Li cycling tests.
As shown in Fig. 3h and Fig.

S13, with the incorporation of MPE, the Li||Cu cell presents superior cycling stability and smaller overpotential with a stable coulombic efficiency of 98.5 % over 300 cycles, meaning the significantly enhanced reversibility and suppressed side reactions between electrolyte and Li metal during the Li stripping/plating process.
The morphologies of Li metal after 300 cycles were further tested.
A rough surface full of bumps and hollows are visualized on the Li surface for the CE system, whereas the Li surface in the STE is tight and smooth (Fig.

A more uniform Li deposition insinuates the great potential of good Li compatibility imparted by MPE solvent, which favors Li+ diffusion on the surface of Li anode and amelioration of the overpotential.
This is also reflected by a thinner thickness of the deposited Li on Cu collector (Fig.

Additionally, irrespective of the low or high current density, the symmetrical Li||Li cell in the STE works with a smaller overpotential in contrast with the unstable stripping/plating potential observed in the CE (Fig.
S16a, b, d), substantiating the superior Li stripping/plating process.
When the cur­ rent density increases to 3 mA cm−2, the cell with CE shows obvious short-circuit phenomenon, while STE can still work normally.
Mean­ while, it can be clearly observed that after adding MPE, the over­ potential decreases significantly (Fig.
The satisfactory performances of Li||Li cells further confirm the encouraging application prospect of MPE in constructing highly stable and effective interface.
Moreover, the observed Li foils surface morphology in symmetrical Li|| Li cells reaffirms the regulation effect of MPE on the Li anode (Fig.

Furthermore, finite element analysis was performed to probe how the MPE would influence the Li morphology and we found that the Li deposition morphology shows a more obtuse angle with the presence of MPE (Fig. 3g, Fig.
S12), suggesting that the MPE could realize a more favorable Li striping/platting process.
In addition, a more uniform electrolyte concentration distribution is observed in the finite element simulation, indicative of a relieved polarization.
Besides the compatibility between the STE and Li anode, the kinetics of SRR was further studied by the ab-initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) simulation [44].
As can be seen in Fig. 4a, the free energy surface (FES) derived from the AIMD results in the CE system performs a ragged shape while the STE shows a smoother one.

Notably, when inspecting the Li+ diffusion route into the PS monomer, we found there are so many local minima and energy barriers in the FES where the Li+ cations are easy to get trapped into the local minima, meaning the decelerated SRR process.
In sharp contrast, Li+ can easily enter the PS monomer in the STE, vividly demonstrating the accelerated kinetics of SRR process (Fig. 4b).

The FES simulation results strongly prove that the decrease in carbonchain length induces a reduced steric hindrance for the accessibility of Li+ to the PS monomer, which accelerates the sulfur transformation during SRR process.
The accelerated SRR dynamics is also proved by the in-situ EIS measurements (Fig. 4c, d, Fig.

Altogether, by intro­ ducing MPE, the STE constructs a kinetically favorable reactor to ignites the whole solid–liquid-solid electrochemistry of sulfur.
According to the guidance of the above theoretical simulations and experimental results, the impact of solvent stereochemistry on Li-S batteries was further studied using coin cells.
Cyclic voltammetry (CV) measurements at different scan rates within a voltage window of 1.7–2.8 V were first conducted to compare the Li+ diffusion and reaction kinetics [50,51].
The STE substantially relieves polarization potential by synchronously raising the cathodic peak potential and reducing anodic peak potential (Fig.

Despite the modulation in solvation structure with the addition of MPE solvent, typical lithiation/delithia­ tion processes of Li-S batteries are still observed in the CV curves, which is different from the traditional sparingly solvating electrolyte that supports a solid-state conversion reaction [35,43,52].
In addition, as the scan rate increases, there is a gradual increase in the peak current in­ tensity for both the electrolyte systems while the peak shape almost remains unchanged.
Therefore, a linear relationship between the peak current (Ip) and the square root of the scan rate (v) can be obtained in the two systems, as shown in Fig.

According to the Randles- Sevcik equation: Ip = 2.69 × 105n1.5AD0.5 Li CLiv0.5 where n is the number of charges, A is the geometric area of the elec­ trode, and CLi represents the concentration of Li+, the diffusion coeffi­ cient of Li+ (DLi +) can be calculated from the linear fitting of Ip versus v0.5.
As shown in Fig. 5a, STE displays the sharper slopes, corresponding to higher DLi + values at the main cathodic and anodic peaks (Fig. 5a).
These results indicate that the Li+ diffusion in the whole cell of STE surpasses that of CE.
Besides, the rapid Li+ diffusion enabled by faster de-solvation process also promises a better Li2S deposition performance.
S20, the cell with STE has a faster deposition rate and the deposition morphology shows a three-dimensional growth mode.
By contrast, the cell with CE shows a slower two-dimensional mode.
The rapid Li+ diffusion, faster deposition rate, and SRR dynamics are propitious to the rate performance especially at high current rates (Fig. 5b).
Specially, when the current density returns to 0.5C, the capacity almost recovers to the same capacity level as the initial cycling number at 0.5C, donating a superior reversibility.

Remarkably, when the current density increases to an ultra-high rate of 5C (Fig. 5c), the retention rate of STE still keeps a decent level while the capacity of CE decays rather fast.
The achieved performances in terms of cycling per­ formance and rate capability are comparable with the recently reported electrolyte engineering strategies (Table S4).
The STE performances were further examined in pouch cells to verify the practical application potential.
When the sulfur loading is sharply increased to 5.2 mg cm−2 and the electrolyte/sulfur ratio is decreased to 5.0 μL mg−1, the cells deliver an initial capacity as high as 1070 mAh g−1.
The energy density of the pouch cell is calculated to be 318.8 Wh kg−1.
After 80 cycles, the cells still harvest 770 mAh g−1 (Fig. 5d), showcasing great application prospect in advanced Li-S batteries.
Considering the fact that the high conductive graphene (HCG) employed is a nonpolar host material without any elaborate mediation (Fig.
S23-25), we believe that there’s much room for the improvement of electrochemical performance in this STE system.

Considering the fast SRR dynamics originated from the better desolvation kinetics, lower viscosity, and inhibited side reactions in the STE system, the performances of STE in gelid conditions were evaluated to further exploit its potential in wide-temperature applications (Fig.
The cells with STE can still operate well under −30 ◦C even at 3C while the cell with CE almost stagnates when the current density is elevated to 1C.
Especially, the cell with CE exhibits a sloping and short second discharge plateau in the charge/discharge profile (Fig.
S27a), which can be indicative of the inhibited pathway of solid–liquid-solid transformation in SRR owing to the tardy Li+ diffusion and SRR process [53,54].
In comparison, the cell with STE still exhibits the traditional discharge behavior, albeit with the appreciable polarization voltage (Fig.
S27b), clearly manifesting the enhanced redox kinetics in STE.

Importantly, the cells with STE could stably operates under −30 ◦C for 100 cycles at 0.5C (Fig. 5e), whereas the cells with CE exhibit signifi­ cantly degraded capacity attainment, incarnating the great application potentials over wide-temperature conditions for STE.

To better understand the appealing superiorities of STE in Li-S electrochemistry, we conducted ex-situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) mea­ surements to track the speciation evolution of the solid sulfur species during the discharge/charge process.
As the discharge proceeds, the Li2S and S8 signal in the CE show an inappreciable variation (Fig. 6a) [55,56], signifying the slow transformation from S8 to Li2S.
In contrast, the Li2S signal in the STE gradually increases, accompanied by the gradual decreases in S8, indicating an ideal S transformation and ener­ getically favorable SRR process (Fig. 6b).
Moreover, this alternant emergence and disappearance of S8 and Li2S species is more pronounced in the subsequent charge process for STE system compared with that in CE.

Although the PS dissolution is suppressed, the Li-S dynamics in STE still outperforms the CE due to the reduced steric effect which reduces the steric hindrance to construct the accessible Li+ diffusion channel to the PS.

Given that the morphology of the cathode plays a crucial role in reflecting the intricate interplay between the electrolyte and the elec­ trode, the cells after cycling in Li-S batteries were disassemble to analyze the impact of STE on the interface.

This is primarily attributed to the decomposition reactions occurring within the electro­ lyte during cell operation, resulting in the deposition of substantial byproducts.

This distinctive morphology is largely attributed to the relatively fewer side reactions associated with STE.
Therefore, STE furnishes a more stable cell oper­ ation environment, minimizing the decomposition of the electrolyte and the formation of deposits.
As a result, STE promote the structural integrity and uniformity of the cathode morphology.
The Li anode surface of the cycled Li-S cells was also analysed by Xray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) to gain a deeper understanding of the enhanced electrochemical performance.
In the F 1 s spectra, we observed an increase in the content of both C-F and Li-F species with the presence of MPE (Fig. 6c, d).

In virtue of the high ion conductivity, high surface energy, and high mechanical strength, the accumulation of abundant LiF species is instrumental to the passivation of Li surface and mitigation of adverse parasitic reactions between PS and Li anode, both of which contribute to the effective Li anode protection and inhibition of dead lithium [45].
In addition to the increased LiF content, we also detected a significant presence of Li3N species on the cycled Li surface in cells with STE (Fig. 6e, f).

Given the higher ionic conductivity and sur­ face energy of Li3N compared to those of LiF, the coexistence of Li3N and LiF reasons the formation of a compact and smooth SEI layer, thus effectively inhibiting the corrosion and consumption of Li anode, in congruence with our observations in Li||Li and Li||Cu cells (Fig.
We further analyzed the S 2p spectra to examine the distri­ bution of sulfur species on the cycled Li surface (Fig. 6g, h).
The peaks at 167.2 and 169 eV corresponds to sulfite/thiosulfate and sulfone groups of TFSI−, hinting the adsorption of TFSI− anions at the solid–liquid interface [57,58].

After deconvolution by Gaussian fitting, we found that the sample exhibits strong signals of bridged sulfur (SB 0, at 163.3 eV, referring to the bridged sulfur atoms in long-chain LiPS) and terminal sulfur (ST 1−, at 161.6 eV, related to terminal sulfur atoms of polysulfide anions Sn2−and sulfur dianions S2−) moieties in the absence of MPE, indicative of severe corrosion and fouling of Li anode due to the shuttle effect of LiPS [58].

In striking contrast, the STE cells show almost inappreciable SB 0 and ST 1− signals, confirming again the effective sup­ pression of both LiPS shuttling and side reactions between PS and Li anode. 4.

Conclusions The stereochemistry-directed solvent molecular design aiming at modulating the local environment of the electrolyte to coordinate weakly with Li+ was proposed to address the comprehensive issues of Li- S electrochemistry.
With weak solvation ability and lowered steric effect of MPE, the STE guarantees a significantly alleviated parasitic reactions between PS and Li anode as well as a promoted kinetics of SRR process.
In virtue of these preponderances of STE, the Li-S batteries with prac­ tically relevant parameters (5.2 mg cm−2 and 5.0 μL mg−1) deliver decent electrochemical performances.
Moreover, benefiting from the better desolvation kinetics, the cell with STE exhibits substantial po­ tential in the application of gelid conditions.
In light of the economy and simplicity, the motif of STE is expected to promote the practical appli­ cation of energy-dense Li-S batteries and even other alkali metal-sulfur batteries.

E-mail address: zbxiao@vip.henu.edu.cn Experimental section Electrochemical measurements: All the cells were assembled in an Ar-filled glove box below 1.0 ppm.
CR-2025 coin cells were assembled in an Ar-filled glove box using the HCG/S-coated aluminum foil as the cathode, lithium foil as anode, and Celgard 2400 as the separator.
The cyclic voltammetry (CV) and electrochemical impedance spectra (EIS) were measured in the CHI660E electrochemical work station.
CV was carried out at a scan rate of 0.1-0.5 mV s-1 within a voltage window of 1.7-2.8 V.
The frequency range of the EIS test is between 100 kHz and 0.01 Hz with 5 mV amplitude.
The frequency cut-off of in-situ EIS measurements 100 kHz-0.01 Hz with 5 mV amplitude.
The value of each discharge depth is shown in Figure S18, each point corresponds to the specific stages that were conducted with EIS measurement in different electrolytes.
The Li2S deposition experiment was measured with assembled cells using carbon paper as the cathode and lithium foil as the anode.
In the cell assembly process, 20 μL electrolyte containing 0.2 M Li2S6 was added on the carbon paper side and another 20 μL electrolyte CE/STE was dropped on the Li foil side.
The cell was first 3 discharged at constant current to the 2.06 V and then discharged with the constant voltage at 2.05 V until the current was below 10−5 A for the nucleation and deposition of Li2S.
Materials Characterizations: The morphologies of Li depositions and Li2S depositions were characterized by scanning electron microscopy (SEM, JSM-7001F).
The SEI components of Li-S cells were further characterized through X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, AXIS, SUPRA+).
X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns were recorded in the range of 2θ = 5-50° on a desktop X-ray diffractometer (RIGAKU-Miniflex II) with Cu Kα radiation (λ= 1.5406 Å).
Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) was measured at a heating rate of 10 °C min-1 using a TAQ600 thermo-gravimetric analyzer.
The Raman measurements of the electrolytes were conducted on a Renishaw inVia device between 200 and 2000 cm-1.
The electrolytes of DME/MPE (1 : 1, by vol.), 0.2 M LiTFSI in DME and 0.2 M LiTFSI in DME/MPE (1 : 1, by vol.) were configured for testing.
NMR analyses were conducted on Varian VNMRS 500 MHz spectrometers. 0.2 M Li2S8 was added to the configured CE and STE electrolytes for testing.
The viscosity of the electrolytes was measured on an TA DHR2 with a controlled shear rate and shear stress at 25 °C.
Ex-situ XRD measurements: HCG/S electrodes were firstly activated at 0.2 C for three cycles.
The cycled electrodes were extracted from coin cells in an Ar-filled glove box and then dried in Ar-filled glove box after washing by DOL/DME mixture.
The cycled electrodes at different charge/discharge state were sealed before the XRD measurement.
Classic MD simulation: Classical molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were performed using the GROMACS MD simulation package version.
The initial configurations were obtained by randomly packing molecules in a periodic cubic box of size 70×70×70 Å3 using PACKMOL.

The initial configuration was first minimized using the steepest descent method, employing a convergence criterion of 1000 kcal/(mol Å), and then using the conjugate-gradient energy minimization scheme, employing a convergence criterion of 10 kcal/(mol Å).
The systems were equilibrated in an isothermal-isobaric ensemble (constant NPT) using a Berendsen barostat to maintain the pressure of 1 bar with a time constant of 2 ps for 2 ns.
All systems were then melted at 400 K for 2 ns and subsequently annealed from 400 to 298 K in three steps for 3 ns.
Finally, production runs of 20 ns were then obtained in the canonical ensemble (NPT) using an improved velocity-rescaling algorithm proposed by Bussi et al. with a time constant of 0.2 ps at 298 K.
The viscosity simulation was performed using another box of 42×42×126 Å3 according to the perturbation method of the reported works.

AIMD simulation: For the CE simulation, single monomer Li2S6 molecules were placed at the center of 16×16×16 Å3 boxes with a 1 : 1 mixture of 10 DME and 10 DOL molecules around occupying the remaining volume of the box.
Likewise, a 3 : 3 : 4 mixture of DME, DOL, MPE was placed around Li2S6 in the other box to simulate the STE environment.
Each of the three Li2S6 monomer systems was solvated with their respective DOL/DME mixtures using the PACKMOL program.

The CP2K software was used to perform optimizations, NVT simulations, and NPT simulations in the same fashion (i.e., same types of basis sets, pseudopotentials, NVT/NPT thermostat, NPT barostat, NVT/NPT temperature, and NPT pressure).
The SHAKE algorithm was used for hydrogen-bearing bonds (1.1 Å for C-H bonds) to extend the time step of the NVT and NPT simulations to 1 fs.
The simulation time for all of the NVT and NPT DOL/DME-solvated Li2S6 system simulations was 5 ps.

Following the NPT simulations, NVT metadynamics simulations were performed on each of the DOL/DME-solvated Li2S6 monomer systems using the final NPT trajectory frame structures and cell lattice parameters.

Each of the metadynamics simulations used two collective variables to scan (1) the monomer sulfur coordination number and (2) the DOL/DME solvent oxygen coordination number of one of the two lithium atoms in each of the Li2S6 monomer systems.

A harmonic wall potential constraint of 1000 kcal/mol was placed on the Li-S distance of the other Li atom (with r0 = 2.7 Å) to allow for the scanning of the free energy of a single Li migration to and from the sulfur chain monomer.

Small repulsive Gaussian hills with a height of 2 × 10-3 Hartree and a width of 0.2 Hartree were added at a frequency of every 50 time steps for both the Li-S and Li-O coordination number collective variables.
Quantum chemical calculation: Quantum chemical calculations were performed using the ORCA 5.0.1 program package.

For the frontier molecular orbital energy, electrostatic energy, the overall reaction energy and the binding energy, B97-3c was first used to optimize the molecular structure for a stable configuration and then r2SCAN-3c was performed to calculate the single-point energy and output molecular orbital state, electrostatic energy state.

For the binding energy, Eb was defined as where the , and refers to the final single point energy of the optimized configuration of the binding state of molecular 1 with molecular 2, the separated state of molecular 1 and molecular 2, respectively.
The parameters of COMSOL Multiphysics: The modeling of Li+ electrodeposition was performed by using COMSOL Multiphysics 5.4 based on the finite element method.
Nernst-Planck-Possion equation was adopted to describe the behaviors of charged ions.
The concentration-dependent Bulter-Volmer equation was employed to introduce the reaction of electrode surface.
Deformed geometry interfaces were applied to the anode and cathode interface and the moving speed of meshes was equal to the deposited rate.
The initial concentration of Li+ was set to 1.0 mol L-1.
The exchange current density was set to be 30 A m-2.
The time of deposition was 2000 s.
